title: The Digital Health Reading Room
description: Plain-language guides, reports, and background reading on digital mental health, organized by topic. A good first stop if you want the bigger picture before choosing anything yourself.

banner.alt: A woman in a red blazer reading a book beside a window

title: Screen Time and Wellbeing: A Classroom Lab
description: A two-period lesson for grades 7–9 that has students trace a day of their own screen use and weigh it against how they felt and slept. Includes discussion prompts, a take-home summary, and a short note for families.

banner.alt: Students at their desks in a classroom as a teacher speaks

title: How Apps Track Mood, and What They Do With It
description: A 10-minute explainer on how mood-tracking apps collect information day to day, what they usually do with it, and what to check before trusting one. Plain visuals, no jargon, and a short list of questions to take away.

banner.alt: A doctor talking with a patient over a video consultation

title: Screens & Feelings
description: A friendly interview series where clinicians, teachers, and parents talk through everyday questions about technology and mental health. Episodes run 20–30 minutes, and the two-part guide to picking a first app is a good place to start.

banner.alt: Two people in conversation on a couch

title: Fernmoor Wellbeing Network
description: A community network for digital wellbeing that keeps a directory of free courses, toolkits, and public talks. The site also publishes a short monthly round-up of new research worth knowing about.

banner.alt: A group meeting around a table with laptops and notes

title: Five Questions to Ask Before Choosing a Mental Health App
description: A practical read that boils app evaluation down to five questions: who made it, what it claims, what it costs, what it can see, and what you get out of it. Written for anyone comparing options for the first time.

banner.alt: A doctor in a white coat talking on a phone

title: Smartphone-Based Support for Anxiety: What the Evidence Says
description: A peer-reviewed review of 41 studies on smartphone-based support for anxiety, summarized for a general audience. Finds modest but consistent benefits, strongest when an app is paired with support from a person.

banner.alt: A doctor in glasses reviewing notes at a desk

title: Sleep Habits Check-In
description: A one-page checklist for looking at evening routines: light, screens, caffeine, wind-down time, and what tends to get in the way. Print it or fill it in on a phone.

title: Getting Started with Health Apps: A Large-Print Guide
description: A step-by-step walkthrough for setting up a first health or wellbeing app, written in large print: choosing, downloading, privacy settings, and who to ask for help. Designed for older adults and the people who help them.

banner.alt: An older man seated on a couch using his phone

title: Harbourlight: Mood and Sleep Journal
description: A private journal for tracking mood and sleep over time, with simple weekly summaries you can share with a counsellor if you choose. No account required, and notes stay on the device.

banner.alt: A person writing in a journal at home

title: Stillbrook: Guided Breathing and Stress Relief
description: Short guided breathing and grounding exercises for stressful moments, with sessions from one to ten minutes. Includes an offline mode for moments with no signal.

banner.alt: A person sitting quietly in a calm room

title: Northwood Calm for Teens
description: An anxiety and mood app designed with teenagers, with check-ins, grounding exercises, and a private space to note what helps. Separate guides are available for parents.

banner.alt: A teenager using a phone on a couch
